events.title: Osborne 1 released
events.summary: Osborne Computer Corporation began shipping the Osborne 1 in April 1981 — the first commercially successful [portable computer].
events.about: The Osborne 1 weighed 24 pounds with a 5-inch screen and dual floppy drives — users carried a complete [CP/M] system between home and office. Its bundled software bundle pioneered the "killer app" sales model. Though short-lived as a company, Osborne proved demand for luggable computers before the [IBM] [PC] dominated portables.

narrative.whyChosen: The Osborne 1 was the first mass-market portable [microcomputer] sold to businesses.
narrative.whyImportant: It established the portable form factor and software-bundle strategy for early [PC] vendors.
narrative.problemSolved: Professionals needed to run business software away from the office without access to a desktop machine.

events.title: Hayes Smartmodem brings PC-controlled dial-up
events.summary: Hayes Microcomputer Products announced the Smartmodem in April 1981 — the first modem a PC could control in software via an RS-232 port and Hayes command set.
events.about: Before the Smartmodem, hobbyists used acoustic couplers or machine-specific modem cards. Hayes put a phone jack and microprocessor on an external box so any computer with a serial port could dial BBSes, UUCP nodes, and early online services. The Hayes AT command language became the de facto standard for dial-up modems through the 56K era.

narrative.whyChosen: The Smartmodem made dial-up networking a plug-in peripheral instead of a custom hardware project.
narrative.whyImportant: It enabled the BBS, dial-up ISP, and remote-admin culture that preceded always-on broadband.
narrative.problemSolved: Microcomputer owners needed a modem that worked across brands without per-machine hardware designs.
